============================================================
Empirical Research Plan – Conscription and Long-Run Earnings
============================================================

1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------
Instrumental‐Variables (2SLS) design.

Why IV?  
•  The military lottery in the Netherlands randomly assigned *draft eligibility* (Z).  
•  Actual service (D) is only *partially* determined by Z – medical deferments, education, conscientious objection, etc. ⇒ non-compliance.  
•  To recover the causal effect of *serving* (not merely being eligible) on later earnings we instrument D with Z.  
•  The first stage (Z → D) satisfies relevance, and the random lottery satisfies exogeneity, giving a credible Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) for compliers.

2. Treatment and Control
------------------------
Treatment variable (endogenous):  
Dᵢ = 1 if individual i actually performed compulsory military service; 0 otherwise.

Instrument:  
Zᵢ = 1 if lottery number ≤ quota cut-off in cohort c (draft‐eligible), 0 if > cut-off.

Control group: men with Z = 0 (high lottery numbers) serve as the counterfactual; they resemble treated men in expectation because Z is random.

Treatment timing: service occurs at ages 18–20; outcomes (earnings, employment) observed annually thereafter.

Notation: cohort c = year of birth × lottery year, so the cut-off varies by cohort.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------
A1. Relevance – P(D=1|Z=1) ≠ P(D=1|Z=0).  
  • Plausible; historical quotas conscripted ~60-70 % of low-number men vs <15 % of high-number men. Will test with first-stage F-stat.

A2. Independence – Z is randomly assigned and independent of potential outcomes.  
  • Guaranteed by publicly supervised lottery; we will verify balance on pre-determined covariates (parental income, birth municipality).

A3. Exclusion – Z affects outcomes only through military service.  
  • Plausible: the lottery draw had no direct economic consequences other than conscription risk. We will probe by checking outcomes measured *before* service (placebo years).

A4. Monotonicity – No one who would serve if *not* drafted refuses when drafted (no “defiers”).  
  • Institutional rules (mandatory call-up) make downward defiance highly unlikely.

A5. Stable Unit/Treatment Value (SUTVA) – one man’s lottery number does not influence another’s earnings.  
  • Reasonable; quotas were large relative to cohort, peer spill-overs minimal for long-run earnings.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
-------------------------------------------
T1. Selective non-compliance beyond medical grounds (e.g., schooling deferments).  
   • Include rich pre-determined covariates; estimate complier characteristics; test heterogeneity.  
   • Report both reduced-form (ITT) and 2SLS to show robustness.

T2. Differential migration or mortality linked to Z.  
   • Use administrative population registers that track emigrants/deceased; include them with zero earnings or use inverse-probability weights; show robustness to sample restrictions.

T3. Measurement error in service status (D).  
   • Rely on Ministry of Defence records; cross-check against personnel files where possible.  
   • Any remaining classical error biases OLS toward zero; IV corrects it.

5. R Code Outline
-----------------
```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)    # fast load
library(fixest)        # iv_ regression
library(modelsummary)  # nice tables

# 1. Load & merge -----------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("nl_conscription_admin.csv")   # one row per man

# 2. Variable construction --------------------------------------------------
# draft quota cutoff differs by cohort -> have lottery_no and quota
dt[, Z := as.integer(lottery_no <= quota_cutoff)]      # instrument
dt[, D := served]                                      # endogenous treat
dt[, ln_earn := log(earnings + 1)]                     # outcome
dt[, cohort := yob]                                    # year of birth
dt[, age := year - yob]                                # if panel

# 3. Main spec --------------------------------------------------------------
# 2SLS with cohort FE and controls
iv_formula <- ln_earn ~ Z | D | cohort +                 # cohort FE
               factor(birth_province) +                  # region FE
               parental_income + education_pretreatment  # controls

est_main <- feols(iv_formula,
                  data = dt, 
                  clusters = ~cohort)                    # cluster by cohort

etable(est_main, se = "cluster")

# 4. First-stage F-stat -----------------------------------------------------
fs <- feols(D ~ Z | cohort + factor(birth_province) + parental_income + education_pretreatment,
            data = dt, clusters = ~cohort)
summary(fs)$ivfstat

# 5. Balance check (placebo) -----------------------------------------------
bal <- feols(parental_income ~ Z | cohort, data = dt)
summary(bal)

# 6. Robustness: leave-one-cohort-out ---------------------------------------
cohort_list <- unique(dt$cohort)
robust_cohort <- lapply(cohort_list, function(cc){
    feols(iv_formula, data = dt[cohort != cc], clusters = ~cohort)
})
```

6. Expected Results
-------------------
Human-capital theory predicts an earnings penalty: service interrupts education and early labour-market experience. Based on prior studies (e.g., −2 % to −7 % long-run wage effect in Europe), I expect:

• ITT (Z) effect: ≈ −1.5 % average annual earnings.  
• 2SLS LATE for compliers: ≈ −4 % to −6 %.

Employment probability may fall slightly or show no effect once earnings conditional on employment are captured.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument relevance  ………………… 1  
C2: Instrument exogeneity ………………… 1  
C3: Exclusion restriction ………………… 0.8 (plausible but untestable)  
C4: Monotonicity …………………………… 1  
C5: No interference (SUTVA) ……………… 1  

Overall ≈ 4.8 / 5.

============================================================
